title: 1 Moment Of Time: Silentville
text: Again this is a tough one as to whether to choose Yes/No to recommend. It's ok. It has a few achievements which encourage you to play it again. Some of the puzzles are pretty creative, and the storyline is fine as is the voice acting. What really prevents me from recommending it, however, are the way the hidden object scenes have been created. The inventory and menus end up getting in the way of the pictures which were clearly done before the inventory and menus were added. This means that you're often looking for items which you can barely see because they have been covered by the inventory. This means that you're desperate for hints or you have to randomly click on everything - particularly anything at the bottom of the screen. This might be deliberate to force you to play again and again for achievements, but if that's the only way anyone will play again you're really scraping the bottom of the barrel. I did spend a couple of hours on it so it was interesting enough to complete it, but I can't say that I really want to play it again, even to get all the achievements.

title: 1 Moment Of Time: Silentville
text: This is one of those games that needs a "neutral" button. Really Good Stuff: The hidden object screens are fun - and very unusual.  Most objects are in two pieces, not just undersomething or inside something. And they are not dependent on solving them in a special order, which is very nice. Some of the mini games were fun.  Clever without being too difficult and there were serveral very unusual types, not just the standard ones. The Story was nice, and for once no violance in the story-line, which I appreciated. Just people making the wrong turning. There was actualy quite a lot of substance to the game.  Especially when you concider the price.  I've paid more for games that took less time to get through than this one. OK Stuff: The music and graphics and voice acting were OK and pretty standard for this type of game. Not So Good - to frustrating: Most of the time the Hint button would just drop you in a different screen - and then take forever to load. We have gotten used to a Map system that let us know where the next step is. This was very lacking. The Worst Things: Sometimes, and far too often, objects you need for the HOG were under the center Inventory strip - and that made finding them next to impossible. The map does NOT take you to a room - it drops you outside of a building, which you have to enter and then move to the different rooms inside. The exit/go back arrow didn't work too well and it was often eaiser to go to the map and then find the right room. Which was pity. Conclusion: Not at all bad. Not Artifex Mundi, but for 1/10th of the price, without being on sale, not a bad buy.

title: 12 Labours of Hercules
text: Short, easy, but fun!  This game is a casual resource management strategy game.  You start each level with one or two workers who travel on set pathways and gather resources.  But they also use resources to clear debris and to build bulidings like a farm.  In later levels you have to carefully choose from multiple pathways to start out otherwise you run out of resources.  When there's a heavy boulder in your way you can call upon Hercules to get his lazy♥♥♥♥♥out of his hammock and heft the boulder out of the pathway.  Some levels have other characters that help you out like Medusa (yes, she's an ally in this game, not an enemy!), Cerberus, Cyclops, and Pegasus. The levels are timed but it only matters if you want to get all the achievements and get the gold rating on all levels.  I found them very easy to complete in plenty of time for the gold rating.  I only had to go back to redo a few levels to get gold. There are some "boss" levels which consist of Hercules alternating shooting arrows at enemies and using his strength to move boulders out of the way or break chains.  There is one really cool boss level where instead of fighting you have to gather specific ingredients to make a healing potion.  There are fruits and colorful potions scattered about and it tells you which specific one you need each time. The levels do not take much time to complete, a few minutes, so it scratches that itch for quick build management strategy when I don't want to take the time to play a long involved game. Can't wait for the sequel!

title: 12 is Better Than 6
text: The developers have removed options with updates, whether it is somethings as "rudimentary" as a brightness slider, to something as essential as difficulty options, it doesn't matter, it isn't here anymore... The game isn't that long, about an two hours or so, although that's relative, depending on how you bode with the difficulty of the game, and how much patience can you have to withstand the terrible ammo management, and weapon system. Basically, this game tries to create the illusion that you're holding, and using, an actual gun by making you &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; the weapon before each shot, this is done by forcing the player to press and hold the right mouse button between each shot, it is as tedious as it sounds, and depending on how tolerant you are, it might be something that either makes your experience better, or "tears" it completely. For me it was, sadly, the latter. Not only that but you don't pickup ammo by walking on top of the weapons, nor by interacting with them while they're on the ground, the only way to aquire ammunition is by unloading each weapon manually, you do this by holding the right mouse button, before trading your weapon for another, of the same kind, or otherwise. It is an utterly terrible system, that I can't stand, it slows down the action to a point where the tension, and adrenaline from gunfights turns into a tedious "micro-management" mess, it is completely unnecessary, and it doesn't contribute anything other than negative aspects to the gunplay. It wouldn't matter nearly as much up until you began noticing the game at times doesn't provide weapons, instead in makes things a bit more diverse by having some later levels offer melee weapons such as shovels, axes, or pickaxes for you to kill your enemies. All of which are useless against any kind of armed enemy, that can, and will, shoot you from afar. Similarly to Hotline Miami what's really going to kill you in this game is your own unawareness to the enemy positions, and where exactly is it that they're coming from to begin with, as well as your own accuracy. Difference being that in Hotline Miami each level was carefully revised to work in line with its own gameplay mechanics, whilst in this one, the game favors much more the concept, and the aesthetic of each level, while not caring in the least about how its own mechanics will work in conjunction with its level design, nor "black and white" aesthetic. What ends up happening is that half of the times you will be confusing enemies for other objects around you, or alternatively, you'll grind your way through the game while trying desperately to actually see in other rooms that are covered by ceilings that don't allow you to see what's inside the actual buildings their sheltering to begin with. Remember, this is a "top down shooter" meaning you will always be secluded to seeing the entirety of the game from that perspective. Then there's the framerate, and the performance, I have a gtx 970, paired with an i5 6600k processor, and 24gb of ram, the game has a very limited graphics, and perfomance options, with only v-sync being the one that caught my eye (I personally hate input lag). Besides that you have resolution options, and presets that go from high to low, that's it... Even while going to the lowest setting, even while starting the game with the option to run it at a lower resolution, which it turn made things clearer, literally, I don't know why. The game still at later levels drop to 40 fps, independently of the setting I chose. I do not recommend this game, I finish it, but it was a "slog" to go through, at the last level, ironically, I chose to go to the "level select" screen to see how many more hours of grueling tediousness I was about to withstand by my own will. I was happy to see I only had one level to finish. And if you're asking to yourself why is it that I imposed myself the completion of this game. Is simple. This is a difficult game, but I'm not complaining because I die, I'm complaining because the game has inherent flaws in its design that end up going a long way in making it a difficult, and tedious experience to complete, even the "picking" of weapons doesn't work well at times, yet the game has created a context in which if you can't pickup a weapon fast enough, you'll get shot by the rushing enemies that are coming aggresively towards you. Even then, some people will claim I'm bashing it because of its difficulty, yet I finished the game. It is just like any other difficult game. If you spend enough time, question what's killing you, and you can do something about it, you'll finish it through. Because videogames, mechanically, don't require anything other than a "mechanical" effort, like the one from a machine that can learn patterns, amongst other things... That process tho, doesn't mean it will be in every game a positive experience in the least. And this is a perfect example of one it isn't.

Due everything being B&W, the enemies are also often very hard to spot from the scenery, which will kill you countless times. First the game felt fun, but while each and every stage in Hotline Miami has its own characteristics and is tied to the story in some way, in this game you feel that you are playing the same stage over and over and over again. It gets really repetitive, really fast.  While contantly dying in Hotline Miami gets your adrenaline pumping and addicted you to it, here it only annoys you after a while, since never you get the same feeling of a "reward" as you get when completing a hard stage in HM. You just move into another identical stage and continue shooting baddies.

title: 2064: Read Only Memories
text: This is the closest thing I've seen to a modern Neuromancer. It's very smartly written, and the writer(s) clearly know their tech. I kept waiting to roll my eyes at some 'Hack the Gibson' moment, but that never came. Everything was plausible, and cyberpunk references ahoy.  The characters are all their own people. The tags are wrong - this is in no way a Visual Novel. It's an excellent Sierra old style point and click adventure. And that's the one possible negative thing - if you find yourselves bored by those, you'll be bored by the downtime looking around here, but I loved it.  Everything's got custom look and use text. And like the best sci-fi, this is fairly forward looking. It's got some things to say about gender, species, body hacking, AI, and genetic modification that seem fairly grounded but amazing. This is some crazy stuff at first blush, but it could definitely happen. And some of it even seems inevitable. tl;dr this is the best I've played on Steam in quite a while.

title: 2064: Read Only Memories
text: After seeing this game recommended by Extra Credits, I was excited to try it out.  Cyberpunk and hard sci-fi have always been fascinations of mine, and it's rare these days to see a game that does a lot with that kind of setting and refuses to drown it out with fancy shootbangs and whatnot.  Even better, it explores a lot of how the concept of personhood and identity would change based on advancing technology and the opening of social norms.  It clearly sides with progress and representation and, just as importantly, does it with grace and nuance.  That was easily the greater part of what made my journey through Neo-SF such a pleasure. On the presentation side, the pixel graphics are charming, the beep boops are easy to listen to and distinctive without being obtrusive, and the music is great chiptune stuff.  It works, and that's great. If there is one downside for me, it's that I'm not the type to aim for any of the other paths you can take through the game, so the replay value for me is kind of low.  Still, with smooth and stable running even on an old laptop and all to show off the kind of story I've been wanting to see more of in games?  Sign me up.

title: 2064: Read Only Memories
text: As someone who this game is firmly targetted at, I gotta say, I'm not terribly impressed. The animations and art style are really the only selling point I can think of, other than that it really is just unfun. I guess my biggest problem is that the protagonist just isn't likeable; the game opens up with them complaining about writing a review for a set of headphones, and goes into how they're "selling their soul bit by bit." This just screams to me of an obnoxious privledged person. Maybe that's the point, to show how they grow as a character, but it really doesn't do you any favors that this is who you're supposed to connect with, especially when you're at the other end of the spectrum. But the game would almost make up for having a poorly written and unlikeable protagonist if the other characters were actually any good. Turing, your robot buddy, is a smug ♥♥♥♥er who can't ♥♥♥♥ing stop talking about how great they are. There's a cat lady who gets super offended at you when you're forced, by the game, to ask if she's a character you're looking for. Then there's goddamn Tomcat, a guy who is nostalgic for the pre-Civil War south. You know, the south that had slaves. Yeah. He's not super likeable either, surprisingly! Then there's the plot. Oh my god the ♥♥♥♥ing plot. Never have so many words been used to say so little. Your friend Hayden is missing and your new robot buddy comes to you for help finding him! Oh boy! Excitement! But its all lost in the sea of words, as Turing just keeps talking and talking and TALKING about♥♥♥♥♥♥you legit do not care about. Here's another issue I have: maybe don't have a nameless protagonist and just have the main character be Turing? That way you're never being talked at for what feels like hours and being told how much of an idiot chump you are. Oh and we'd also feel some sort of emotional connection to Hayden (he did create Turing after all!) instead of having a protagonist that just goes along with events because they have nothing  better to do with their time. Oh and don't even get me started on the comparisons between the LGBTQ+ community and the weirdo hybrids. Not only does this have the most infantitle understanding of how gene therapy would work (sharks can get cancer you morons!), but the oppression the hybrids claim to experience just feels so false. "We wanna have kids!" they scream, "but this law says we can't!" That law is set in place because hybrids would have literal monstrosity babies that would probably die within a few days, because baby octopus-human-fox hybrids could not survive outside the womb. Not to mention the strain it would take on the mother, both physically and mentally. The only actual case of oppression in the game is of a cat lady having some of her non-gene therapy'd eggs being destroyed by racist doctors, but even then the courts side with her and give her a huge pay out! The system works! That's not oppression! I guess that's a lot of words to say I think this game is garbage. Its garbage plain and simple. The writing is awful, the characters are awful, and the message is awful. Its awful and I'm glad I got it as a gift so that I didn't give money to the developers. If you want a game with lots of talky stuff that isn't awful, but also wanna support indie devs, there's plenty of other options that don't make you want to remove your eyes with a rusty spoon. May I suggest Analogue: A Hate Story?

title: 2064: Read Only Memories
text: Read Only Memories is an adventure-esque visual novel about the first sentient true AI. So far so good. The art design is retro and the story itself isn't that bad at all, if it wasn't for some particular parts and content I personally hadn't any issues with but which I believe to possibly have a negative impact on most players. While being an open-minded indiviual having no gripe with pretty much anything the art and indie industry could throw at me, I need to point out that there is a massive amount of 'new-age-genderism' within the game. Out of the roughly dozen of characters from the main cast, half of them is gay (no big deal) and / or transgender (for example a bearded man named Sympathy, consistently refered to as 'she'). There's also genetically engineered furries (I kid you not) and the ability for the main character to pick his/her/its/their/xes/zis personal denominator (or a custom one, you can literally make up yourself) that the game will continue using consistently. And while I am totally open-minded about all of the above, I think it was deliberately put in there not because of necessity, but because some of the developers are super deep into that kind of scene (had to chuckle when I read that Zoe Quinn also worked on this in the credits), which makes the whole setting come over a lot more weird than it would have been necessary story-wise. The main companion, sentient AI Turing, is also abysmally annoying and childlike, with a very strong emotional moral compass, which isn't exactly what I personally would consider a realistic take on a newly formed sentient mechanical conscience and the game does miss a lot of opportunities to get philosophical within the boundaries of its main theme. It also tries to pitch in as many tropes at any given time as possible, which might be your cup of tea, but started to personally annoy me after the dozenth pop-reference within five sentences. What it yet does depict is a world completely different from hours, set about 40 years into the future. And while in some regards being quite over the top in a way that Gamergate was 'mildly' over the top, I'm even willing to believe that the world could be and look like that in a couple of decades, even although it definitely wouldn't be my personal favourite of possible outcomes. So in regard to a recommendation: While being an interesting little game with five branching story paths, your tolerance level for homosexuality, transgenderism, transhumanism, and whatever you would scientifically call genetically altered humans to become true furries should be exceptionally high, otherwise you probably will get mad quite often throughout the game. And even if you can easily be okay with all of that, the remaining game is a very simple and dialogue heavy visual novel with average writing and average written characters, railroading you towars plot twists that aren't twists at all and fulminating in some of the most unspectacular endings I have ever seen within visual novels. All in all I didn't regret playing this, but I don't believe I can recommend it to anyone, let alone the general public.

title: 3079 -- Block Action RPG
text: 3079 was the first game developed by phr00t that i played, it was a few years ago on Desura. To this day its still my favorite game in phr00t's lineup, its a real gem of a game, a mix between Borderlands and Terraria (some will say Minecraft instead of Terraria but i never played Minecraft so i cant argue either way). Surprisingly the game is still as addictive today as it was several years ago. Its an open world game. Its a first person shooter/melee (you can use melee weapons and tools too). It has decent rpg elements, you can level stealth, stealing, charisma, mining, engineering (crafting), strenth and energy. The itemisation is really great, and the fact you can expand it with an interesting upgrade system (engineering/crafting), makes it even more satisfying than Borderlands or Diablo. You can mine for resources (and a lot of the environment is destructible), you can build a decent amount of stuff (bases, storage, home teleports, elevators). Can get plenty of quests and information from the npcs, can get followers who will help in combat, can get on friendly or hostile terms with factions. The graphics are basic but even after several years i still like them, dont know if its because they grow on me or its just nostalgia, but regardless, this is a gem of a game that for me is just as addictive today as it was the first time i played it, and thats no small thing.

text: I was sold from the video, it looks great. Minecraft with guns and a grappling hook! Like Just Cause 2 in Minecraft. What's not to love? It is like Minecraft with guns made in Java. Before the developer was done with this game, he was already hyping up the sequil. This is great for a first time developer. It is a simple Minecraft with guns. The guns work well enough, the enemies are giant and easy to hit. When you die, that's it. You crash back to the launcher. Speaking of the launcher, that's the only way to adjust the settings. Including controls. This is probably the 2nd worst button configuration I've ever seen. You select what the key does, then you find the key from a drop down list. When you set a key, chances are it unsets another key that has nothing to do with the key you just set. Such as if I set something to use the 'Right Key' then I set something to the 'Enter Key' it will set the previous 'Right Key' to the 'F2 Key.' Huh? Again, this is clearly someone's first game. With all that being said, the game generates a random world and yet always starts you suspended high above the ground in orbit, suspended. When you find out the gravity button to drop you from the sky you might die on impact. It is quite unforgiving. If you survive the fall through the use of the gravity button, you're immediately in hostile territory. Sometimes the floating red monsters will murder you before you even land. From the start, the guns are underpowered. When you run out of ammo, you start losing health when you shoot. An understanding of enemy levels would have been nice, such as a beginner enemy should take one or two bullets. Then as you progress they take more bullets and then you find better guns or upgrade so they take less bullets. The only redeeming factor about this game is multi-player, but really, if you're playing with friends any game will be fun, because you and your friends will always have fun. That's why they're your friends. There are far better FPS games, which this is a FPS. I can't even call it Minecraft, since there's not much crafting or world craftability as there is with Minecraft. I just can't recommend this game. It is also very telling when a game took so long to be Greenlit.

text: Just bought the game on Steam and holy damn does it look good. Not only does the world feel organic and full of dangers, but there's solid gameplay utilizing the best parts of both the building of Minecraft and item-searching in dungeon-diving of rogue-likes. Also, it looks good 'n artsy. None of that Minecraft monotone but rather some creepy and original style to it. Randmization really makes stuff interesting in this game. There's definitely lots to see, meet and explore. As to the difficulty, it's the game's strong point. This world is relentless and does need you to take it seriously. You need to acquire skill first, then items in order to survive and advance in progress-indicating levels and power. But what I'm really looking forward to is what's in the future of the game. It does seem it could easily get some servers with communities similar to those of DayZ in order to make the game feel even more organic, purposeful and alive. Not to mention patches and mods. It's a world ever at war. And you need to shape it.
